title: Weekly Reading Rundown - What People Have Been Writing This Week
author: Sarah Findlater
summary: In this weekly curated digest, Sarah Findlater shares six education Substack posts she found worth reading, each with a short editorial gloss connecting the piece to a recurring theme in her own thinking about evidence and practice. She highlights Mary Myatt's distinction between precision and accuracy in Key Stage 3 assessment data, Carl Hendrick's argument that retrieval practice must be planned through curriculum design rather than bolted onto lessons, and Adam Boxer's case that schools should strengthen universal classroom provision before reaching for labels or separate interventions. She also flags Robert Pondiscio's launch of 'The Practice Project,' a joint AEI/researchED initiative translating cognitive science into practical guidance for teachers, alongside two AI-focused pieces: Eric Hudson's examination of default settings in AI-infused schools, and Mark Fraser's argument that frictionless ed-tech can quietly remove the productive struggle that constitutes learning. Findlater's own curatorial framing -- favoring pieces that connect evidence to classroom consequence rather than abstract commentary -- gives the roundup a consistent throughline even though the six pieces span assessment, curriculum design, inclusion, research translation, and AI policy.
points: On Myatt: her distinction between precision and accuracy is spot on -- a grade can look exact while hiding differences in task difficulty, marking and curriculum content.

On Hendrick: adding a quiz to the start of a lesson can look reassuringly evidence-informed, but it tells us very little unless the content has been chosen for a reason and pupils need it again later.
On Boxer's 'Good schools first': schools need to strengthen universal provision before reaching for labels, reduced curricula or separate interventions when a pupil is struggling.

On Pondiscio's Practice Project: a new AEI/researchED collaboration aiming to turn education research into professional knowledge teachers can use, starting with papers on explicit instruction and transferable skills.
Findlater closes each edition with an open invitation for readers to submit pieces, noting she reads every submission fully before recommending it.
quotes: Just sharing some posts I have enjoyed reading that have inspired me, made me think deeply or made me laugh.

Mary Myatt writes about the comfort a precise-looking number often gives us. Her distinction between precision and accuracy is spot on: a grade can look exact while hiding differences in task difficulty, marking and curriculum content.
Carl Hendrick argues that retrieval practice needs to be planned through the curriculum, with deliberate routes back to earlier knowledge.

Adam Boxer poses the idea that schools to need to strengthen universal provision before reaching for labels, reduced curricula or separate interventions when a pupil is struggling. He suggests that real inclusion is rarely so neat.
Robert Pondiscio introduces The Practice Project, a collaboration between AEI and researchED that aims to turn education research into professional knowledge teachers can use.
Eric Hudson goes beyond the usual list of AI tools and asks schools to examine the choices behind them. He looks at devices, student agency, AI policies and infrastructure.
Mark Fraser shares a practical way to judge whether technology has removed unnecessary difficulty or removed the work through which learning happens.
If you have found an excellent free education post on Substack, send me the link. I'll read the whole thing before I recommend it.
